title: 1.1 What is Data?
content:
### What is Data?
Data is a collection of raw, unorganized facts, figures, symbols, or observations that can be processed to produce meaningful information. In computing, data is represented in binary format and structured in databases.

title: 1.2 What is Database?
content:
### What is a Database?
A database is an organized collection of structured data stored electronically in a computer system. Databases are controlled by a Database Management System (DBMS).

title: 1.3 DBMS Introduction
content:
### Introduction to DBMS
A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that manages databases, allowing users to store, retrieve, update, and organize information efficiently while ensuring data integrity.

title: 1.4 Database vs File System
content:
### Database vs File System
Unlike traditional file systems, a DBMS handles data redundancy, concurrency control, security, data integrity, and complex queries seamlessly.

title: 1.5 Advantages of DBMS
content:
### Advantages of DBMS
Key benefits include: minimized data redundancy, data sharing, data consistency, transactional safety, secure access, and backup & recovery services.

title: 1.6 Types of Databases
content:
### Types of Databases
Databases are categorized into Relational (RDBMS), NoSQL (Key-Value, Document, Graph), Distributed, Cloud, and Object-Oriented databases.

title: 2.1 Tables, Rows & Columns
content:
### Tables, Rows & Columns
In a relational database, data is organized into tables (relations), where columns represent attributes and rows (tuples) represent individual data records.

title: 2.2 Keys
content:
### Keys in Relational Databases
Keys uniquely identify rows in a table. Types include Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, Super Keys, Candidate Keys, and Composite Keys.

title: 2.3 Constraints
content:
### Integrity Constraints
Constraints enforce database rules. Examples include: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, and DEFAULT.

title: 2.4 ER Model
content:
### Entity-Relationship Model
The ER Model describes database structures using Entities, Attributes, and Relationships, serving as the blueprint for relational designs.

title: 2.5 ER Diagram
content:
### Entity-Relationship Diagrams
ER diagrams visually represent entity relationships, detailing attributes, primary keys, and cardinality (1:1, 1:N, N:M).

title: 3.1 SQL Introduction
content:
### SQL Introduction
Structured Query Language (SQL) is the standard language to manage and query relational databases, divided into DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL.

title: 3.2 CREATE
content:
### CREATE Statement
The DDL CREATE statement builds databases, tables, indexes, or views: `CREATE TABLE users (id INT, name VARCHAR(100));`

title: 3.3 INSERT
content:
### INSERT Statement
Inserts new records into a table: `INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES (1, "Alice");`

title: 3.4 SELECT
content:
### SELECT Statement
Retrieves columns from a table: `SELECT * FROM users;`

title: 3.5 UPDATE
content:
### UPDATE Statement
Modifies existing records matching a condition: `UPDATE users SET name = "Bob" WHERE id = 1;`

title: 3.6 DELETE
content:
### DELETE Statement
Removes records matching a condition: `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1;`

title: 3.7 WHERE
content:
### WHERE Clause
Filters records conditionally: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id > 5;`

title: 3.8 ORDER BY
content:
### ORDER BY Clause
Sorts results ascending or descending: `SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY name DESC;`

title: 4.1 GROUP BY
content:
### GROUP BY Clause
Groups rows sharing identical values: `SELECT category, COUNT(*) FROM products GROUP BY category;`

title: 4.2 HAVING
content:
### HAVING Clause
Filters group results (unlike WHERE which filters rows): `SELECT category FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;`

title: 4.3 JOINS
content:
### SQL JOINS
Combines columns from multiple tables. Types: INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN.

title: 4.4 UNION
content:
### UNION Operator
Combines query results into one distinct list: `SELECT id FROM customers UNION SELECT id FROM employees;`

title: 4.5 Subqueries
content:
### Subqueries
Queries nested inside other queries: `SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);`

title: 4.6 Views
content:
### Database Views
A virtual table built from a SELECT statement: `CREATE VIEW active_users AS SELECT * FROM users WHERE active = true;`

title: 4.7 Indexes
content:
### Indexes
Structures that speed up query execution: `CREATE INDEX idx_name ON users(name);`

title: 5.1 Functional Dependency
content:
### Functional Dependency
Occurs when one attribute uniquely determines another attribute. Denoted as X -> Y, where X is determinant.

title: 5.2 Normalization
content:
### Database Normalization
Process to structure database schemas to eliminate insertion, update, and deletion anomalies. Forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF.

title: 5.3 Transactions
content:
### Transactions
Executions of SQL statements treated as a single logical unit of work (all-or-nothing execution).

title: 5.4 ACID Properties
content:
### ACID Properties
Ensures transactional safety:
- **Atomicity:** Complete success or total rollback.
- **Consistency:** Moves database from one valid state to another.
- **Isolation:** Concurrent transactions do not interfere.
- **Durability:** Committed changes persist even during power loss.

title: 5.5 Concurrency Control
content:
### Concurrency Control
Manages concurrent transaction conflicts using Locking protocols (shared/exclusive) and timestamp ordering.

title: 5.6 Database Security
content:
### Database Security
Protects data using access control privileges (GRANT/REVOKE), database encryption, and SQL injection prevention.

title: 1.1 Introduction to Version Control
content:
### Introduction to Version Control
Version Control System (VCS) is software that helps software developers track changes to code over time. It keeps a history of modifications, allowing developers to revert files to a previous state, compare changes, and collaborate seamlessly.

title: 1.2 Centralized vs Distributed Version Control
content:
### Centralized vs Distributed VCS
- **Centralized VCS (CVCS):** Uses a single central server that stores all versioned files. E.g., SVN, Perforce.
- **Distributed VCS (DVCS):** Every developer has a full clone of the repository, including its history, on their local machine. E.g., Git, Mercurial.

title: 1.3 Why Git
content:
### Why Git?
Git is the most popular distributed version control system. It is fast, handles branches efficiently, operates offline, and ensures data integrity through SHA-1 cryptographic hashing of commits.

title: 1.4 Why GitHub
content:
### Why GitHub?
GitHub is a cloud-based hosting service for Git repositories. It adds collaboration features like Pull Requests, Code Reviews, Issues, Projects, Actions (CI/CD), and team management.

title: 1.5 Installing Git
content:
### Installing Git
Install Git on your system:

- macOS: `brew install git`
- Windows: Download from git-scm.com

title: 1.8 Personal Access Tokens
content:
### Personal Access Tokens (PAT)
PATs are fine-grained tokens that act as passwords for HTTPS-based authentication. Learn to create PATs in Developer Settings on GitHub with specific scopes.

title: 1.9 git init
content:
### git init
Initialize a new local Git repository in the current folder. This creates a hidden `.git` directory containing configuration databases.

title: 1.10 Git Lifecycle
content:
### The Git Lifecycle
Files in a Git repository move between states:
1. **Untracked:** New files not added to index.
2. **Unmodified:** Tracked files with no changes.
3. **Modified:** Tracked files with changes not staged.
4. **Staged:** Changes marked to be committed.

title: 1.11 git status
content:
### git status
Shows the status of files in the current working directory, including untracked, modified, and staged files.

title: 1.12 git add
content:
### git add
Stages modified or untracked files, moving them into the staging area (index) ready to be committed.

title: 1.13 git commit
content:
### git commit
Saves staged changes permanently to local history with a descriptive commit message.

title: 1.14 git log
content:
### git log
Displays the history of commits in the repository, including hash, author, date, and commit message.

title: 1.15 git diff
content:
### git diff
Compares differences between unstaged modifications and the last committed files.

title: 2.1 Create Repository
content:
### Creating a GitHub Repository
Navigate to GitHub, click the "+" icon, select "New repository", define name, visibility (public/private), and initialize with README/gitignore.

title: 2.2 Remote Repository
content:
### Remote Repository
Remote repositories are hosted online (e.g. GitHub). They allow team members to synchronize local work using push, pull, and fetch operations.

title: 2.3 git remote add origin
content:
### git remote add origin
Links your local repository to a remote server on GitHub. The default alias name is `origin`.

title: 2.4 git push
content:
### git push
Uploads local commits to a remote repository branch.

0.description: Push local main to origin and set upstream

title: 2.5 git pull
content:
### git pull
Fetches remote changes and merges them directly into your current local branch.

0.description: Fetch and merge origin main changes

title: 2.6 git fetch
content:
### git fetch
Downloads remote history updates to local reference database without modifying your current code workspace files.

title: 2.7 git clone
content:
### git clone
Downloads an existing repository from GitHub to your local machine, initializing and checking out the main branch.

title: 2.8 Git Branches
content:
### Git Branching
Branches allow you to isolate development work (like implementing feature/bugfix) without disrupting the production-ready `main` code branch.

title: 2.9 git switch
content:
### git switch
Easily switch branches or create new feature branches.

1.description: Create and switch to a new branch

title: 2.10 git checkout
content:
### git checkout
Traditional branch switching and file restoration command.

title: 2.11 git merge
content:
### git merge
Combines the commit history of a source branch directly into the current branch.

title: 2.12 Pull Requests
content:
### Pull Requests (PR)
PRs are GitHub features that propose changes from a feature branch to `main`. They provide a workspace for discussion and reviews before merging.

title: 2.13 Code Reviews
content:
### Code Reviews
Reviewing code ensures code quality. Developers leave inline comments, request revisions, or approve the changes.

title: 2.14 Reviewers
content:
### Reviewers
Assign other developers to review your Pull Request. Codeowners can be configured to automatically request reviews from designated experts.

title: 2.15 Labels
content:
### Labels
Categorize Pull Requests and Issues (e.g. `bug`, `enhancement`, `wip`, `documentation`) for easy filtering.

title: 2.16 Milestones
content:
### Milestones
Group Issues and Pull Requests toward a specific target release date or project phase.

title: 3.1 Merge Conflicts
content:
### Merge Conflicts
A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile overlapping modifications made to the same lines in a file across merging branches.

title: 3.2 Conflict Resolution
content:
### Resolving Conflicts
Locate conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`), edit the file to preserve the correct lines, save, and stage the file.

title: 3.3 git restore
content:
### git restore
Discards unstaged modifications in your working files, reverting them back to the last committed index.

title: 3.4 git reset
content:
### git reset
Resets repository state back to a past commit. Soft leaves changes staged; mixed (default) leaves changes unstaged; hard deletes all changes.

0.description: Undo last commit, leave changes unstaged

1.description: Undo last commit and delete changes

title: 3.5 git revert
content:
### git revert
Creates a brand-new commit that applies the exact opposite changes of a specified commit, preserving repository commit history securely.

title: 3.6 git stash
content:
### git stash
Temporarily shelves (stashes) your unstaged modifications so you can work on a clean directory, and restore them later.

title: 3.7 Git Rebase
content:
### Git Rebase
Applies commits from a branch on top of another branch base. It creates a linear history by updating the base of your branch.

title: 3.8 Interactive Rebase
content:
### Interactive Rebase
Allows reordering, editing, squashing, or dropping commits in a command interface.

title: 3.9 Squashing Commits
content:
### Squashing Commits
Combines multiple small commits into a single descriptive commit (often via interactive rebase or merge squashing) to maintain a clean git history.

title: 3.10 Cherry Pick
content:
### git cherry-pick
Selects a single specific commit from another branch and applies its changes directly onto your current branch.

title: 4.1 README.md
content:
### README.md
The landing page of a repository. It provides documentation on how to build, run, and configure the project.

title: 4.2 Markdown
content:
### Markdown syntax
Markdown is a lightweight markup language. E.g. `# Header`, `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `[Link](url)`, `` `code` ``.

title: 4.3 LICENSE
content:
### Project Licenses
Specifies what permissions and restrictions apply to code redistribution and usage (e.g. MIT, Apache 2.0, GPL).

title: 4.4 .gitignore
content:
### .gitignore configuration
A text file listing patterns of files and directories (like `node_modules/`, `.env`, build/ outputs) that Git should completely ignore.

title: 4.5 GitHub Issues
content:
### GitHub Issues
Track bug reports, feature requests, and tasks. Integrates labels, assignees, and milestones.

title: 4.6 Project Boards
content:
### Kanban Boards
Kanban-style boards to manage task workflows. Drag tasks between columns: "To do", "In progress", "Done".

title: 4.7 GitHub Pages
content:
### GitHub Pages hosting
Free hosting for static websites directly from a GitHub repository (e.g. docs, portfolio).

title: 5.1 CI/CD
content:
### CI/CD Foundations
- **Continuous Integration (CI):** Automates building and testing code changes.
- **Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD):** Automates releasing code to production servers.

title: 5.2 GitHub Actions
content:
### GitHub Actions
A built-in automation engine in GitHub to run workflows triggered by events (e.g. push, pull_request).

title: 5.3 Workflow Files
content:
### Workflow files
Workflows are stored inside the `.github/workflows/` directory as `.yml` files.

title: 5.4 YAML
content:
### YAML Syntax
YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) is key-value based, indentation-sensitive, human-readable structure.

title: 5.5 Jobs
content:
### Jobs
Workflows consist of one or more jobs that run in parallel by default (can be set to run sequentially).

title: 5.6 Steps
content:
### Steps
Jobs contain a sequence of steps. Each step executes a shell command or runs a predefined action.

title: 5.7 Runners
content:
### GitHub Runners
Virtual machines (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS) hosted by GitHub that execute the workflow jobs.

title: 5.8 Automated Testing
content:
### CI Automated Testing
Configure actions to run `npm test`, `pytest`, or compilation verification steps automatically on PR submit.

title: 5.9 GitHub Secrets
content:
### Encrypted Secrets
Store API keys and deploy tokens securely in repository settings, accessing them via `${{ secrets.MY_TOKEN }}`.

content:
### GitHub Codespaces
A cloud-hosted VS Code environment built directly into GitHub. Accessible inside any browser.

title: 6.2 Dev Containers
content:
### Dev Containers
Define development environment parameters (dependencies, OS, extensions) inside a `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` file.

title: 6.3 GitHub Copilot
content:
### GitHub Copilot
An AI-powered pair programmer assistant. Suggests code lines and blocks directly inside the editor.

title: 6.6 Secret Scanning
